conclusion.justification: The report explicitly concludes that the claim is false and misleading, citing multiple scientific studies, physiological measurements, and fact-checks showing that cloth and surgical masks do not cause dangerous CO2 buildup.
conclusion.label: rejects

report:
**Conclusion: The claim is false/misleading.** Multiple studies and fact-checks find that cloth or surgical masks do not cause dangerous CO2 buildup or hypercapnia in healthy wearers, including those with lung disease such as COPD.

A study on "Effect of Face Masks on Gas Exchange in Healthy Persons and Patients with COPD" found no significant differences in oxygen or CO2 levels with or without masks, even in people with severely impaired lung function (https://www.foxnews.com/health/face-masks-dont-cause-carbon-dioxide-build-up-or-restrict-breathing). A 2020 measurement study found CO2 concentrations under masks during normal activities were comparable to or lower than levels people already tolerate during everyday tasks like office work (2200 ppm), far below hazardous thresholds (https://aaqr.org/articles/aaqr-20-07-covid-0403.pdf). A more recent systematic review and meta-analysis of N95 and surgical masks concluded that while N95s modestly raised CO2 slightly more than surgical masks during activity, "overall no big difference from no mask" was found — key evidence against claims of dangerous buildup (https://www.rimpacts.com/rd/p?c=10021879917).

Fact-checking organizations reached the same conclusion. AFP Fact Check, Reuters, USA Today, and the Associated Press all rated the hypercapnia claim false or misleading after consulting health experts, noting that mask materials are porous enough that CO2 escapes readily and does not accumulate to harmful levels (https://factcheck.afp.com/prolonged-use-face-masks-unlikely-cause-hypercapnia).

While some low-quality or non-peer-reviewed sources (e.g., blogs referencing a "German study" on stillbirths) claim otherwise, these are not supported by credible scientific literature and have been widely debunked. The scientific consensus, based on physiological measurements and clinical studies, is that properly worn cloth or surgical masks do not cause dangerous CO2 buildup, even with prolonged use.
